## Abstract

The blood-brain barrier (BBB) presents a major challenge for delivering large molecules to study and treat the central nervous system. This is due in part to the scarcity of targets known to mediate BBB crossing. To identify novel targets, we leverage a panel of adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) previously identified through mechanism-agnostic directed evolution for improved BBB transcytosis. Screening potential cognate receptors for enhanced BBB crossing, we identify two targets: murine-restricted LY6C1 and widely conserved carbonic anhydrase IV (CA-IV). We apply AlphaFold-based in silico methods to generate capsid-receptor binding models to predict the affinity of AAVs for these identified receptors. Demonstrating how these tools can unlock target-focused engineering strategies, we create an enhanced LY6C1-binding vector, AAV-PHP.eC, that, unlike our prior PHP.eB, also works in *Ly6a*\-deficient mouse strains such as BALB/cJ. Combined with structural insights from computational modeling, the identification of primate-conserved CA-IV enables the design of more specific and potent human brain–penetrant chemicals and biologicals, including gene delivery vectors.

---

A conserved receptor is identified as a target for engineered vectors to deliver therapeutics to the brain from the bloodstream.

## INTRODUCTION

The blood-brain barrier (BBB) presents a fundamental bottleneck for the delivery of effective research tools and therapeutics to the central nervous system (CNS) ([*1*](#R1)–[*3*](#R3)). This complex structure, composed mainly of brain endothelial cells along with pericytes, astrocytes, and microglia ([*2*](#R2), [*4*](#R4)), prevents the passage of large molecules, including gene delivery vectors, such as adeno-associated viruses (AAVs). Some can cross by receptor-mediated transcytosis ([*5*](#R5), [*6*](#R6)); the rest must be delivered via invasive intracranial injections or technically challenging focused ultrasound ([*7*](#R7)). The rational design of BBB-crossing large molecules has long been hampered by our imperfect understanding of the mechanisms involved in transcytosis, with only a handful of targets, such as transferrin receptor ([*8*](#R8)–[*11*](#R11)), validated for research and therapies ([*6*](#R6), [*12*](#R12)–[*14*](#R14)).

Directed evolution is a powerful method for generating biomolecules with enhanced fitness for desired properties even with incomplete understanding of the underlying biological systems ([*15*](#R15)). The outcomes of directed evolution libraries can in turn be used to unlock previously unknown biology by probing the mechanism of action of molecules with evolved properties. We decided to apply this paradigm of reverse-engineering directed evolution hits to the accumulating wealth of AAV libraries selected for CNS enrichment after systemic administration ([*16*](#R16)–[*25*](#R25)).

One such improved rodent BBB–crossing AAV capsid is PHP.eB ([*26*](#R26)), which we previously identified by applying Cre recombination–based AAV targeted evolution (CREATE) ([*17*](#R17)) to the AAV9 parent capsid ([*27*](#R27), [*28*](#R28)). Following systemic injection in genetically divergent mouse strains, PHP.eB can show either potent CNS tropism (as in C57BL/6J, FVB/NCrl, and DBA/2J) or behavior akin to AAV9 (as in BALB/cJ) ([*29*](#R29)–[*31*](#R31)). This is explained by the receptor for PHP.eB, the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)–anchored protein LY6A, being strongly expressed in C57BL/6J (the directed evolution selection host), FVB/NCrl, and other mouse strains but nonfunctional in the BALB/cJ strain and other mammals ([*32*](#R32)–[*34*](#R34)). Consistently, in nonhuman primates (NHPs) that lack functional LY6A, PHP.eB and related capsids display limited, AAV9-like CNS infectivity ([*29*](#R29), [*35*](#R35)–[*37*](#R37)). As AAVs have become the vector of choice for human gene therapies, including for the CNS ([*38*](#R38)–[*40*](#R40)), complications from directly applying mouse-evolved AAVs in diverse genetic backgrounds has contributed to a shift toward performing AAV directed evolution in NHPs. In so doing, researchers hope to increase the likelihood of identifying AAVs whose enhanced tropism will translate to humans.

As both preclinical validation and, increasingly, selection of engineered AAV capsids occur in NHPs ([*37*](#R37), [*41*](#R41), [*42*](#R42)), problems arise. The animals’ scarcity ([*43*](#R43), [*44*](#R44)) and cost slow the identification of promising capsids, and the risk of species-specific AAVs (that behave differently in NHPs and humans) entering clinical trials remains. Nevertheless, examples are beginning to accumulate not only of capsids that can cross both rodent and NHP BBB ([*37*](#R37)) but also, importantly, of ones that can cross the macaque but not the rodent BBB ([*42*](#R42)). Collectively, this diverse set of capsids engineered over the past decade by many groups represents, through their yet-unexplored mechanisms of action, an unprecedented opportunity to start discovering targets for crossing the BBB across strains and species.

Here, we demonstrate a path forward to identifying BBB-crossing mechanisms by understanding how brain-tropic AAVs, such as those previously identified by directed evolution in mice ([*20*](#R20), [*22*](#R22), [*24*](#R24), [*37*](#R37)), reach their destination from the bloodstream. Focusing on AAVs whose enhanced CNS infectivity upon systemic injection in mice is conserved across strains ([*20*](#R20), [*22*](#R22), [*24*](#R24)), we identified two receptors for potent BBB crossing by engineered AAVs: murine-restricted LY6C1 and primate-conserved carbonic anhydrase IV (CA-IV). As a proof of concept for receptor-informed directed evolution, we targeted LY6C1 to generate AAV-PHP.eC, a mechanistically distinct BBB-crossing AAV for murine models lacking functional LY6A (e.g., BALB/cJ). To further unlock target-driven vector engineering strategies, we used a recently developed computational approach ([*45*](#R45)) that uses AlphaFold-Multimer ([*46*](#R46), [*47*](#R47)) to screen peptides against potential receptors in silico and generated interaction models of AAVs and their receptors that are challenging to solve experimentally and that may inform human BBB-crossing drug development.

## RESULTS

### Identification of engineered AAVs that do not use LY6A

LY6A is the receptor responsible for the enhanced CNS tropism of PHP.B and PHP.eB in mice ([*32*](#R32)–[*34*](#R34)), and one strain-specific single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) disrupts its GPI-anchored membrane localization ([Fig. 1A](#F1)) ([*34*](#R34)). Previously, we applied our M-CREATE directed evolution selection platform to a library of AAV9 variants (with seven-amino-acid insertions at position 588 of capsid variable region VIII) and identified a family of engineered AAVs with diverse CNS tropisms and a shared sequence motif, typified by their founding member, AAV-PHP.B ([Fig. 1B](#F1)) ([*22*](#R22)). The variants’ enhanced CNS potency is lacking in BALB/cJ mice, a phenomenon explained by their shared reliance on LY6A for BBB crossing ([*32*](#R32)–[*34*](#R34)). Recently, multiple engineered AAVs outside the PHP.B sequence family which retain their enhanced CNS tropism in BALB/cJ mice were identified ([*20*](#R20), [*22*](#R22), [*24*](#R24)). Before attempting to find cognate receptors for these AAVs, we first sought to confirm their independence of LY6A.

To directly probe potential LY6A binding interactions, we performed surface plasmon resonance (SPR). To ensure the detection of even weak interactions, we dimerized LY6A by fusion to Fc, immobilized it at high density on a protein A chip, and tested each AAV analyte across a range of concentrations ([Fig. 1C](#F1)). As expected, AAV9 showed no evidence of binding at any concentration, and PHP.B sequence family members all showed strong binding interactions with LY6A. While precise affinities could not be determined because of the effects of avidity and mass transport, the interaction profiles were consistent with subnanomolar affinities. Conversely, all BALB/cJ-enhanced engineered AAVs were indistinguishable from AAV9, exhibiting no detectable interaction with LY6A.

### Construction of a cell culture screen for putative receptors of engineered AAVs

Reasoning that a receptor that engineered AAVs can co-opt for efficient BBB crossing is likely to be both highly expressed and highly specific to the endothelial cells of the brain, we analyzed previously collected single-cell RNA sequencing data from dissociated C57BL/6J brain tissue ([Fig. 2A](#F2)) ([*48*](#R48)). We investigated gene expression levels within CNS endothelial cell clusters and differential expression compared to most other CNS cell type clusters. Genes were filtered to select only those annotated in UniProt as localized to the plasma membrane before calculating their endothelial cell differential expression score in Scanpy. This score was then plotted against each transcript’s mean abundance, revealing a long tail of highly expressed and highly specific CNS endothelial membrane proteins. Encouragingly, *Ly6a* appeared at the far end of this tail. From this analysis, we selected a panel of 40 abundant and specific candidate receptors (table S1).

S1A) ([*34*](#R34)). Hypothesizing that this property is likely to be conserved among BBB-crossing receptors, we made this behavior the basis of a receptor transient overexpression screen ([Fig. 2, B and C](#F2)). We cloned the C57BL/6J coding sequence of each of the 40 candidate receptors into a mammalian expression plasmid and tested each against engineered AAVs in triplicate at two different doses ([Fig. 2, A and D](#F2)). PHP.eB and *Ly6a* served as a positive control.

As expected, we found that all members of the PHP.B sequence family showed a marked boost in infectivity in *Ly6a*\-transfected cells compared to untransfected cells, while *Ly6a*\-independent AAVs performed identically in both conditions ([Fig. 2, D and E](#F2), and fig. S1B). The infectivity of all *Ly6a*\-dependent capsids was boosted to a similar extent (fig. S2B).

### Identification of LY6C1 and CA-IV as receptors for BBB crossing of *Ly6a*\-independent engineered AAVs

We observed boosts in infectivity for all tested *Ly6a*\-independent AAVs with previously unidentified receptors ([Fig. 2D](#F2)). Unexpectedly, given their different sequence families, all of the initial *Ly6a*\-independent AAVs responded to the same candidate receptor, *Ly6c1* ([Fig. 2, D to G](#F2), and fig. S1B). In addition, despite its *Ly6a*\-dependent pattern of CNS infectivity across murine strains ([*22*](#R22)), PHP.N also exhibited enhanced infectivity in *Ly6c1*\-transfected cells. At a higher dose, PHP.N outperformed both AAV9 and PHP.eB in CBA/J mice (fig. S3), which express a GPI-disrupted LY6A. While polymorphisms in *Ly6c1* exist between mouse strains \[as shown by a published analysis of the 36 mouse strains for which whole genomes are available ([*34*](#R34))\], we found that, unlike *Ly6a*, none of the polymorphisms were predicted to disrupt GPI anchoring of LY6C1 to the plasma membrane using PredGPI ([*49*](#R49)). To determine the specificity of the LY6C1 interaction, we performed a follow-up screen with additional closely related and CNS-expressed LY6 superfamily members and found no cross-reactivity of *Ly6c1*\-dependent AAVs with other LY6 proteins ([Fig. 2G](#F2)). CAP-B10 and CAP-B22, which have seven amino acid substitutions in capsid variable region IV and show enhanced potency in adult marmosets ([*37*](#R37)), did not exhibit any additional receptor interactions that would explain their NHP tropism in either of the screens described above or a third screen with marmoset CNS-expressed LY6 family members (fig. S2C) nor did any LY6-interacting AAV cross-react with the recently described human LY6S, a close relative of murine LY6A ([Fig. 2G](#F2)) ([*50*](#R50)). While we used validated candidate receptor clones (table S1), it is possible that lack of membrane expression could result in a false negative in our screens.

We also expanded the LY6 follow-up screen to include a second set of seven previously identified engineered AAVs (9P) ([*24*](#R24)), which yielded an additional five LY6A and LY6C1-interacting AAVs ([Fig. 2G](#F2)). The 9P AAVs 9P31 and 9P36, however, did not display enhanced infectivity with any LY6 protein in the panel and so were tested on the full receptor panel ([Fig. 2D](#F2)). Both 9P31 and 9P36 displayed an infectivity boost with the GPI-linked enzyme CA-IV (encoded by *CA4* in human and *Car4* in mouse) ([Fig. 2D](#F2) and fig. S1B). This interaction was specific to CA-IV among membrane-associated CAs ([Fig. 2G](#F2)). As with *Ly6c1*, polymorphisms in *Car4* across mouse strains are not predicted to affect GPI anchoring to the plasma membrane ([*34*](#R34), [*49*](#R49)). Unlike mouse-restricted *Ly6a* and *Ly6c1*, *CA4/Car4* is conserved throughout vertebrates, including NHPs and humans ([*51*](#R51)–[*53*](#R53)). Therefore, we chose to confirm our screen results in vivo using *Car4* knockout (KO) mice (B6.129S1-Car4tm1Sly/J, the Jackson Laboratory (JAX), strain no. 008217). Immunofluorescence confirmed that CA-IV is strongly expressed throughout the brain vasculature of homozygous wild-type (WT)/WT mice and completely absent in KO/KO ([Fig. 3A](#F3)). When dosed with 3 × 1011 viral genomes (v.g.) per animal, PHP.eB, 9P31, and 9P36 all strongly expressed in both the brain and liver of WT mice ([Fig. 3B](#F3)). Under the same conditions in KO/KO mice, PHP.eB was unaffected, whereas both 9P31 and 9P36 completely lack enhanced CNS tropism ([Fig. 3C](#F3) and fig. S3B). On the other hand, liver tropism, which is governed by AAV9’s naturally evolved receptor interactions, was decoupled from this effect, with all three viruses showing strong transduction in KO/KO mice.

#### Fig. 3. CA-IV is required for the CNS potency of *Car4*\-dependent AAV.

[![Fig. 3.](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/69c9/10115422/b5cd7bf8c6e9/sciadv.adg6618-f3.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=10115422_sciadv.adg6618-f3.jpg)

[Open in a new tab](figure/F3/)

(**A**) Immunostaining for CA-IV in the brains of WT/WT and KO/KO *Car4* mice. Magnified regions from WT/WT demonstrate endothelial expression across diverse brain regions. (**B**) AAV-PHP.eB, 9P31, and 9P36 packaging mNeonGreen under the control of the ubiquitous CAG promoter were intravenously administered to WT/WT *Car4* mice at a dose of 3 × 1011 v.g. per animal (*n* = 3 per condition). Three weeks after administration, transgene expression was assayed by mNeonGreen fluorescence throughout the brain and liver. (**C**) AAV-PHP.eB, 9P31, and 9P36 packaging mNeonGreen under the control of the ubiquitous CAG promoter were intravenously administered to KO/KO *Car4* mice at a dose of 3 × 1011 v.g. per animal (*n* = 3 per condition). Three weeks after administration, transgene expression was assayed by mNeonGreen fluorescence throughout the brain and liver. Scale bars, 2 mm.

Notably, every AAV we tested showed a moderate boost in infectivity in cells transfected with *Slco1c1* (also known as *Oatp1c1*), an integral membrane anionic transporter ([Fig. 2D](#F2)). Unlike for other potential receptors, however, the mNeonGreen signal was weak and diffuse, extending beyond cell boundaries (fig. S1C), suggesting a transgene export or cell health phenotype. The universality of this effect and the specificity of *Slco1c1* expression in the brain suggest a possible role in the weak BBB transcytosis of parent AAV9. None of the other 36 candidate receptors produced a meaningful infectivity boost for any of the 16 engineered AAVs screened.

### Directed evolution of an improved *Ly6c1*\-dependent capsid

Next, we aimed to demonstrate a proof of concept for receptor-targeted directed evolution. For this purpose, we chose the murine receptor LY6C1 (versus the human CA-IV) due to prompt availability of (i) strains with clear BBB differences, e.g. LY6A, and (ii) diverse Cre-transgenic animals for M-CREATE selections that, for now, are not available for CA-IV in other species. In addition, given the mixed backgrounds of preclinical animal models, it remains important to have mechanistically distinct gene delivery vectors for rodents. We therefore sought to engineer a single optimized capsid for broad adoption as a research tool in GPI-disrupted LY6A mouse strains, a still unmet need, using the M-CREATE method we previously developed for AAV capsid directed evolution ([*22*](#R22)). This method uses Cre-dependent AAV genome recovery from desired tissues and cell types after in vivo selection in Cre-transgenic mice and allows deep characterization of selected capsids across various cell types and tissues.

Using M-CREATE, we constructed scanning 3-amino-acid substitution capsid libraries in the chemically diverse LY6C1-interacting variants PHP.C1, PHP.C2, PHP.C3, and PHP.C4 and pooled these libraries for two rounds of selection in Syn-Cre mice ([Fig. 4A](#F4)). In the second round of selection, we also included Olig2-Cre, Tek-Cre, and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP)–Cre mice, as well as WT C57BL/6J and BALB/cJ mice, so that we could detect potential differences in enhancement between these strains or cell types during selection among the variants ([Fig. 4B](#F4)). While PHP.C2 variants dominated both rounds of selection in the C57BL/6J background (Cre-dependent or not), PHP.C1 variants dominated the round 2 Cre-independent selection in BALB/cJ (fig. S4). Following selection, we individually produced and characterized top-performing variants. AAV-PHP.eC (variant 19), evolved from PHP.C1, retained LY6C1 interaction in cell culture ([Fig. 4C](#F4)) and outperformed PHP.C2 in multiple mouse strains with membrane-disrupted LY6A ([Fig. 4D](#F4)). Immunohistochemistry confirmed that PHP.eC strongly infects neurons and astrocytes across strains (fig. S5A). PHP.eC thus provides a potent tool for transgene delivery in mouse strains without membrane-localized LY6A.

#### Fig. 4. Engineering an enhanced *Ly6c1*\-dependent AAV.

AAVs were pooled, and two rounds of M-CREATE selections were performed in 6- to 8-week-old Cre-transgenic mice. (**B**) Round 2 selection brain enrichments for diverse Cre-transgenic and WT mice of selected control AAVs and 20 capsid variants selected for further study. Yield was determined during small-scale production for final screening across strains. (**C**) Potency in cell culture infectivity assay of PHP.eB, PHP.C2, and PHP.eC (variant 19) in HEK293T cells transfected with mock (none) or *Ly6c1* receptor cDNA, demonstrating that PHP.eC retains LY6C1 interaction. (**D**) PHP.C2 and PHP.eC packaging mNeonGreen under the control of the ubiquitous CAG promoter were intravenously administered to nonobese diabetic (NOD)/ShiLtJ and BALB/cJ mice at a dose of 3 × 1011 v.g. per animal (*n* = 3 per condition). Three weeks after administration, transgene expression was assayed by mNeonGreen fluorescence throughout the brain and liver, demonstrating PHP.eC’s increased potency. Scale bars, 2 mm (sagittal image) and 250 μm (brain region).

### AlphaFold-based methods to identify receptor binding peptides and engineered AAV binding poses in silico

Having identified a panel of receptor and AAV capsid pairings, we aimed to see whether we could capitalize on rapid advances in protein structure prediction to generate binding poses for engineered AAVs and their cognate receptors. We began by applying an AlphaFold-based computational method ([*46*](#R46), [*47*](#R47)) for Automated Pairwise Peptide Receptor Analysis for Screening Engineered AAVs (APPRAISE-AAV for short) ([*45*](#R45)). Inspired by recent work ([*54*](#R54), [*55*](#R55)), this method uses AlphaFold-Multimer to place surface-exposed peptides spanning mutagenic insertions (AA587 to AA594) from two distinct AAV variants in competition to interact with a potential receptor ([Fig. 5A](#F5)). This comprises the minimal peptide that encompasses the solvent-exposed residues of capsid variable region VIII. A combination of physical and geometric scoring parameters that include interface energy, binding angle, and binding pocket depth calculations are used to generate a peptide competition metric. Results from these individual pairwise competitions can be assembled into larger matrices that rank sets of AAV capsid insertion peptides according to their receptor binding probability encoded in the AlphaFold neural network. When applied to the receptors identified in our screens, we found that the experimentally verified LY6A, LY6C1, and CA-IV targeting peptides rise to the top of their respective rankings ([Fig. 5, B and C](#F5)). Some false negatives were also observed, however, as in 9P08 with LY6A or 9P36 with CA-IV.

#### Fig. 5. In silico ranking of AAV variants by their receptor binding propensities.

[![Fig. 5.](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/69c9/10115422/519518414239/sciadv.adg6618-f5.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=10115422_sciadv.adg6618-f5.jpg)

[Open in a new tab](figure/F5/)

(**A**) Overview of AlphaFold-based in silico Automated Pairwise Peptide-Receptor Analysis for Screening Engineered AAVs (APPRAISE-AAV for short) ([*45*](#R45)). Surface peptides from AAV variants are put in pairwise binding competition using AlphaFold-Multimer. A peptide competition metric is calculated according to each peptide’s interface energy, binding angle, and pocket depth (see Materials and Methods for details) before being assembled into broader ranked matrices of interaction likelihood. Competition results reflect the relative peptide binding probability encoded in the AlphaFold neural network. (**B**) Table of engineered AAV capsids, their confirmed receptor, and the capsid peptide sequence used in APPRAISE-AAV. References: 1: Gao *et al.* ([*27*](#R27)), 2: Deverman *et al.* ([*17*](#R17)), 3: Chan *et al.* ([*26*](#R26)), 4: Nonnenmacher *et al.* ([*24*](#R24)), and 5: Ravindra Kumar *et al.* ([*22*](#R22)). (**C**) Matrices ranking AAV peptides by their average competition metric over 10 replicate conditions for LY6A, LY6C1, and mouse CA-IV. AAV peptide labels in bold indicate those experimentally identified to interact with the corresponding receptor. Metric values out of range (−100 to 100) were capped to range limits.

In addition to predictions of whether a peptide binds to a receptor, we can also computationally interrogate the structural details of the binding interaction. We generated binding poses by pairing the top AAV insertion peptide with its receptor and validated the binding pose for each pairing by repeating our cell culture screen with receptors containing point mutations hypothesized to disrupt the high-confidence region of the binding interface \[as determined by the per-residue estimated model confidence–predicted local distance difference test (pLDDT) score and consistency between replicate models\] in these predicted poses.

We began by modeling the interaction of PHP.eB with LY6A so that the wealth of existing experimental data on this interaction ([*56*](#R56)–[*58*](#R58)) could be used to build confidence in these methods before their application to LY6C1 and CA-IV receptor interactions. The PHP.eB peptide is predicted to nestle in a groove in LY6A, forming strong interactions at Pro5′ and Phe6′ ([Fig. 6A](#F6)) with several LY6A residues ([Fig. 6B](#F6)). We therefore introduced a point mutation in this groove, LY6A Ala58Arg, without affecting LY6A membrane localization or antibody epitope, and found that it disrupts PHP.eB’s enhanced infectivity with the WT receptor (fig. S5B). This experimental result further bolsters confidence in APPRAISE-AAV rankings in silico.

#### Fig. 6. Engineered AAV interactions with LY6A.

[![Fig. 6.](https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/69c9/10115422/b98662e4bfe0/sciadv.adg6618-f6.jpg)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/core/lw/2.0/html/tileshop_pmc/tileshop_pmc_inline.html?title=Click%20on%20image%20to%20zoom&p=PMC3&id=10115422_sciadv.adg6618-f6.jpg)

(**A**) AlphaFold-Multimer–predicted LY6A-PHP.eB peptide complex structure. PHP.eB peptide is color-coded by predicted local distance difference test (pLDDT) score, a per-residue estimate of the model confidence. The highest confidence side chains, P5′ and F6′, are shown as spheres. LY6A A58R mutation, chosen to disrupt the predicted peptide interaction, resulted in reduced potency in the cell culture infectivity assay. Extent of infection (max, 0.29; min, 0.03) and total brightness per signal area (max, 0.61; min, 0.16). (**B**) LY6A residues with at least two atoms within 5 Å of the modeled PHP.eB peptide. (**C**) Complete model of the PHP.eB trimer and LY6A complex. The AlphaFold-Multimer structural prediction from (A) was combined with a capsid monomer-receptor structural prediction and optimized using Rosetta Remodel within the context of the AAV trimer (fig. S6A). (**D**) Zoomed-in view of the PHP.eB-LY6A binding interface in modeled PHP.eB-LY6A complex and PHP.eB residues with at least two atoms within 5 Å of LY6A.

To gain a full picture of the AAV-receptor interaction, we next modeled the PHP.eB insertion peptide and LY6A receptor complex within the context of the AAV capsid threefold symmetry spike. This structure is challenging for standard modeling tools because of the large size of an AAV capsid (~200 kDa per trimer) as well as the often weak and dynamic binding interactions between engineered capsids and receptors \[micromolar affinities possible without avidity ([*57*](#R57))\]. AlphaFold-Multimer failed to capture direct contact between fLY6A and PHP.eB capsid in either monomer or trimer configurations. To address this challenge, we developed an integrative structure modeling pipeline. In this pipeline, an initial model of an AAV capsid trimer predicted using AlphaFold-Multimer is structurally aligned with an AlphaFold-predicted model of the receptor with the AAV peptide through the high-confidence Pro5′ and Phe6′ residues of the peptide insertion and RosettaRemodel ([*59*](#R59)) optimization of the linking peptide residues within the context of the AAV capsid threefold symmetry spike (fig. S6A). This complete binding model ([Fig. 6C](#F6)) provides a snapshot for a dynamic interaction that has thus far proven resistant to high-resolution structural characterization ([*57*](#R57)).

The PHP.eB-LY6A computational model is consistent with available experimental results. RMSD (root mean square deviation) between the computational PHP.eB model and a cryo–electron microscopy (cryo-EM)–based model ([*57*](#R57)) \[Protein Data Bank (PDB) ID: 7WQO\] is 0.36 Å. RMSD increases in PHP.eB’s engineered loop to 1.36 Å. The only high-confidence deviation from cryo-EM structures of uncomplexed PHP.eB is the side chain of Phe6′, which shows no substantial electron density, indicating flexibility, but forms a stable interaction with LY6A in our model (fig. S6B, right). The high-confidence prediction of Pro5′ and Phe6′ aligns with recent evidence showing that PFK 3-amino-acid insertion alone is sufficient to gain LY6A binding ([*58*](#R58)). While LY6A can bind any insertion loop of a trimer, additional interactions induce steric clashes, supporting a ratio of one LY6A per capsid trimer. A PHP.eB-LY6A complex ensemble image forced to contain 60 bound copies of LY6A resembles a recently reported cryo-EM map, whose analysis pipeline averaged over all 60 singly occupied binding sites to form a composite map (fig. S6C) ([*57*](#R57)). The computational model shows that a single copy of both LY6A and AAV receptor (AAVR) PKD2 domains may bind to the same threefold spike simultaneously without clashing (fig. S6D), in agreement with saturation binding experiments ([*57*](#R57)). Consistent with previous work showing that the LY6A SNP D63G does not affect PHP.eB binding ([*34*](#R34)), the residue is greater than 10 Å from the PHP.eB peptide atoms in the computational model. The PHP.eB-LY6A complex model includes several interactions involving AAV insertion–adjacent residues, which is consistent with a previous report ([Fig. 6D](#F6)) ([*56*](#R56)).

Having validated the structural modeling methods against experimental data for the PHP.eB LY6A interaction, we next applied them to the receptors identified in this work. Unlike for LY6A and CA-IV, the predicted binding pose for PHP.C2 peptide with LY6C1 was found to vary with the version of AlphaFold-Multimer used, with v1 predictions closely matching mutational data from our cell culture infectivity assay (fig. S6E). This complementarity between versions has been reported previously ([*60*](#R60)). In mouse CA-IV, 9P31 peptide occupies the catalytic pocket of the enzyme ([Fig. 7A](#F7)). The 9P31 tyrosine residue shared with 9P36 approaches the enzyme active site, and 9P31’s divergent tryptophan is situated in an ancillary pocket ([Fig. 7B](#F7)). This predicted binding pose is competitive with the binding site of brinzolamide (PDB ID: 3NZC) ([*61*](#R61)), a broad CA inhibitor that is prescribed for glaucoma ([*62*](#R62)). In the cell culture infectivity assay, brinzolamide shows a dose-dependent inhibition of 9P31 and 9P36 potency, while PHP.eB is unaffected ([Fig. 7B](#F7)). The smaller brinzolamide binds deep in the catalytic core of CA-IV, where side chains are largely conserved between species ([Fig. 7C](#F7)). 9P31 peptide, however, extends to the surface of the enzyme where there is considerable sequence divergence that prevents cross-reactivity across species. Thus, while brinzolamide binds to both mouse and human CA-IV ([*61*](#R61), [*63*](#R63)), 9P31 and 9P36 are selective for mouse CA-IV ([Fig. 7D](#F7)). Chimeric receptors that swap a highly divergent loop of the 9P31 binding site show that this region is necessary but not sufficient to control 9P31 and 9P36 potency. Engineering a human CA-IV–binding AAV with optimal BBB-crossing properties is both critically important and not trivial without ready in vivo model systems for validation, as illustrated by the extensive, multi-year efforts realizing transferrin receptor’s potential ([*8*](#R8), [*9*](#R9), [*64*](#R64)–[*66*](#R66)).

## Abstract

Over the past ∼25 years, structural studies of adeno-associated virus (AAV) capsids have greatly aided our understanding of the biology of these single-stranded DNA viruses and provided insights into their utilization as gene therapy vectors for the treatment of various human diseases. Recent advances in cryo-electron microscopy have yielded a library of currently ∼150 high-resolution AAV capsid structures, with more than 50% determined in the last 5 years alone. Comparative analyses of capsids from primate and nonprimate origins have revealed both conserved architectural elements, such as the canonical jelly-roll fold, and critical surface variations that affect receptor interaction, antibody recognition, and intracellular trafficking. These structures, as well as those in complex with glycan and proteinaceous receptors, purification agents, and antibodies, have been instrumental in rational capsid engineering, guiding the design of new variants with enhanced transduction efficiency, tissue specificity, and reduced detection by pre-existing neutralizing antibodies. This review summarizes the available AAV capsid structures to date, highlighting landmark discoveries over the years, and offers perspectives on how structural biology will continue to drive innovation in AAV gene therapy.

**Keywords:** adeno-associated virus, AAV vector, gene therapy, capsid, receptor, pre-existing antibodies, capsid engineering, cryo-EM, X-ray crystallography

Mietzsch and colleagues review approximately 25 years of structural studies on AAV capsids. They describe the current library of around 150 high-resolution structures, emphasizing how these structural insights have advanced our understanding of AAV biology and guided capsid engineering efforts to enhance the efficacy of AAV vectors for gene therapy applications.

## Introduction

First discovered as a contaminant of laboratory adenovirus preparations in the 1960s,[1](#bib1) adeno-associated viruses (AAVs) are now considered the most promising vectors for *in vivo* gene delivery to treat a wide range of monogenic diseases.[2](#bib2),[3](#bib3) To date, eight AAV-based therapeutics have been approved for commercialization by the European Medicines Agency and/or the Food and Drug Administration: Glybera, an AAV serotype 1 (AAV1) vector for the treatment of lipoprotein lipase deficiency[4](#bib4); Luxturna, an AAV2 vector for the treatment of Leber’s congenital amaurosis[5](#bib5); Zolgensma, an AAV9 vector for the treatment of spinal muscular atrophy type 1[6](#bib6); Upstaza/Kebilidi, an AAV2 vector for the treatment of aromatic L-amino acid (aa) decarboxylase deficiency[7](#bib7); Roctavian, an AAV5 vector for the treatment of hemophilia A[8](#bib8); Hemgenix, an AAV5 vector for the treatment of hemophilia B[9](#bib9); Elevidys, an AAVrh.74 vector for the treatment of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD)[10](#bib10); and Beqvez, an AAVrh.74 variant vector for the treatment of hemophilia B.[11](#bib11) In addition to these commercially approved AAV gene therapy treatments, the number of clinical trials of AAV-based gene therapies has skyrocketed in recent years,[2](#bib2) exceeding 300 clinical trials as of 2025.[12](#bib12)

AAV vectors are derived from viruses of the *Parvoviridae* family, genus *Dependoparvovirus*, which package a ∼4.7 kb linear, single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) genome inside their nonenveloped icosahedral capsids with *T* = 1 symmetry and a diameter of ∼25 nm.[13](#bib13),[14](#bib14) The AAV genomes ([Figure 1](#fig1)) contain two large open reading frames, the *rep* and *cap* genes, which are flanked by two identical inverted terminal repeats (ITRs).[15](#bib15) The *rep* gene encodes up to four Rep proteins (Rep40, Rep52, Rep68, and Rep78) that are important for genome replication and packaging, while the *cap* gene encodes the capsid proteins.[16](#bib16) These include the viral proteins (VPs) VP1, VP2, and VP3, which are expressed at a ratio of approximately 1:1:10.[17](#bib17),[18](#bib18),[19](#bib19) The three VPs overlap at their C-termini, with VP1 (∼82 kDa) containing the sequences of VP2 (∼67 kDa) and VP3 (∼60 kDa).[14](#bib14) The unique N terminus of VP1 is referred to as the VP1 unique (VP1u) region.[20](#bib20) The N-terminal sequence of VP2 shared between VP1 and VP2 is termed the VP1/2 common region.[15](#bib15) The VP1u contains an essential phospholipase A2 (PLA2) domain,[21](#bib21) and the VP1/2 common region contains nuclear localization signals,[22](#bib22),[23](#bib23) both of which are critical in the AAV viral life cycle.[24](#bib24) While VP1 is essential for AAV infectivity, VP1 and VP2 are not required for capsid assembly.[25](#bib25),[26](#bib26) In addition, the AAV genome ([Figure 1](#fig1)) encodes two smaller proteins: the assembly-activating protein (AAP) and the membrane-associated accessory protein (MAAP).[27](#bib27),[28](#bib28)

The AAV genome and its proteins

An overview of the AAV genome is shown, with its two open reading frames flanked by inverted terminal repeats (ITRs), promoters, and polyadenylation site (pA). Below, the expressed Rep proteins are depicted in green, the VPs in yellow, and the smaller membrane-associated accessory protein (MAAP) and assembly-activating protein (AAP) in blue. The VP1 unique (VP1u), the VP1/2-common region (VP1/2), and the structurally ordered segment of the capsid proteins are indicated.

For the generation of AAV vectors, the *rep* and *cap* genes of the wild-type genome are replaced with a transgene vector cassette, and only the flanking ITRs (usually from AAV2) are retained, which act as packaging signals for the recombinant vector genome.[29](#bib29) The Rep proteins (also usually from AAV2) and the VPs (any capsid gene) are expressed in trans.[30](#bib30) Using this setup, the vector genome is packaged into the capsids instead of the wild-type genome.[15](#bib15) Common production pipelines utilize either HEK293 cells or insect Sf9 cells for AAV vector manufacturing.[31](#bib31),[32](#bib32) The selection of the “appropriate” capsid gene is crucial for the resulting AAV vectors, as the generated capsids determine the tropism and antigenicity of the vectors[33](#bib33),[34](#bib34) and can impact the success of a given therapy.

Therefore, substantial research has been conducted on both the characterization and improvement of AAV capsids.[35](#bib35) Determining AAV capsid structures is critical to achieving these goals and is the focus of this review. While structures have also been determined for the nonstructural Rep proteins of the AAVs,[36](#bib36),[37](#bib37) these will not be covered in this review. To date, 155 AAV capsid structures at a resolution ≤ 4 Å have been determined since 2002 ([Figure 2](#fig2)). Until 2016, structural characterizations of AAV capsids were performed using X-ray crystallography. Since then, all AAV capsid structures have been determined using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), largely due to groundbreaking advancements in direct electron detectors and computational processing. Furthermore, AAVs are excellent specimens for cryo-EM studies because of their relatively small size for a virus, icosahedral symmetry, and ability to stably assemble into homogenous particles.[38](#bib38) Currently at 1.56 Å, the structure of AAV-DJ represents the highest-resolution capsid structure, though this may soon be surpassed.[39](#bib39),[40](#bib40) The rapid increase in available AAV capsid structures over the last ∼5 years underscores the need for a comprehensive review to identify current and emerging trends in structural AAV biology.

## The AAV capsid morphology

Early transmission electron microcopy images of AAVs revealed the nonenveloped nature of the viral particles.[41](#bib41) Following the determination of the first capsid structures of various RNA viruses,[42](#bib42),[43](#bib43) icosahedral symmetry was also assumed for AAV capsids.[44](#bib44) The first structural insights into the AAV capsid were obtained from a low-resolution cryo-EM reconstruction of AAV2 at ∼10 Å resolution, which revealed large protrusions surrounding the three-fold symmetry axes and narrow channels at the five-fold axes.[45](#bib45) In 2002 the structure of the AAV2 capsid was determined by X-ray crystallography at 3 Å resolution,[46](#bib46) marking the beginning of structural characterization of AAV capsids. The AAV2 structure, as well as those of other AAV capsids determined thereafter (e.g., AAV5, AAVrh.8, and AAVhu.37) ([Figure 3](#fig3)A), regardless of the method used, showed that only the shared VP3 region (the ∼520 C-terminal aa) is structurally ordered, while the VP1u, the VP1/2 common region, and approximately 15 aa of the VP3 N terminus are not observed.[14](#bib14) This was further confirmed when AAV1 and AAV3 capsids composed solely of VP3 were compared with capsids containing all three VPs. In these cases, the capsids were structurally indistinguishable from one another.[26](#bib26),[47](#bib47) The VP structure of AAVs, similar to that of all icosahedral ssDNA viruses, contains a jelly-roll motif formed by an eight-stranded (βBIDG and βCHEF) antiparallel β-barrel motif[48](#bib48) ([Figure 3](#fig3)B). In addition, the βBIDG sheet is extended by the βA strand, which is situated antiparallel to the βB strand. The β(A)BIDG sheet forms the interior surface of the capsid and is larger than the βCHEF sheet, which is mostly buried inside the capsid. Furthermore, a conserved alpha-helix (αA) is inserted between the βC and βD strands. These secondary elements form the building block of the capsid and are conserved among AAVs and other genera within the *Parvovirinae* subfamily, including *Amdo-*, *Ave-*, *Boca-*, *Erythro*\-, *Proto*\-, and *Tetraparvovirus*, for which structures have been determined.[49](#bib49),[50](#bib50),[51](#bib51),[52](#bib52),[53](#bib53) The surface of the capsid is formed by interconnecting loops between the β-strands. These loops are labeled based on their flanking β-strands—for example, the loop connecting the βE and βF strands is referred to as the EF loop ([Figure 4](#fig4)). In AAVs, the BC, DE, EF, GH, HI, and C-terminal loops contribute to the surface topological features of the capsid.[48](#bib48) The long GH loop, consisting of more than 200 aa, forms several subloops. These surface loops exhibit high aa sequence diversity and structural variability among different AAVs (see [the variable regions of the AAVs](#sec4) section) and among members of the different *Parvovirinae* genera.[49](#bib49),[53](#bib53)

Although the sequences of the VPs from various AAVs differ by up to 50% in aa identity, their capsids share common morphological features.[38](#bib38) To form the icosahedral AAV capsid, 60 VP monomers assemble through 2-, 3-, and 5-fold symmetry interactions.[54](#bib54) These interactions result in the formation of cylindrical channels by five DE loops at the icosahedral 5-fold symmetry axes. The 5-fold channels connect the interior of the capsid to the external environment and are believed to play important roles in genome packaging/ejection, as well as VP1u externalization.[20](#bib20),[55](#bib55),[56](#bib56) Surrounding the 3-fold symmetry axes, the AAV capsids possess large protrusions formed primarily by the GH loops.[57](#bib57) The shallowest regions of the capsid are located at the 2-fold symmetry axes and around the 5-fold pore, to which the C-terminal loop and HI loop contribute, respectively.[58](#bib58) The raised region between these depressed areas is referred to as the 2/5-fold wall, formed by the BC, EF, and partially the C-terminal loops. While all AAVs conserve these overall surface features, different loop conformations and aa sequences lead to alternative appearances of the capsid surface and subsequently result in variable receptor usage, which contribute to distinct host and tissue tropisms as well as antigenic profiles.

## The capsids of primate-based AAVs

The first AAVs isolated from human or nonhuman primate cells and/or tissues were referred to as AAV serotypes. Historically, AAV serotypes were distinguished by serological studies, physiochemical characterizations of their genomes, restriction digestion patterns, and later by their sequences.[59](#bib59),[60](#bib60),[61](#bib61),[62](#bib62) However, following the identification of AAV6, which differs by only six aa from AAV1 in the VP1 capsid sequence,[62](#bib62) an increasing number of AAV isolates were found—due to advancements in sequencing technologies—that also varied by only a few aa from previously described AAV serotypes. Thus, the designation of new AAV serotypes was discontinued after serotype 13, and the AAVs were instead organized into clades. The clade organization of the AAVs was first proposed in 2004, based on more than 100 unique isolates from humans and nonhuman primates (including rhesus monkeys, cynomolgus and pigtailed macaques, baboons, and chimpanzees).[63](#bib63) They are defined based on a neighbor-joining phylogenetic tree of their capsid protein sequences, as the *rep* gene sequences were often not sequenced or deposited. This resulted in the formation of six clades, with the AAV serotypes as prototypic members (clade A: AAV1 and AAV6; clade B: AAV2; clade C: AAV3 and AAV13; clade D: AAV7; clade E: AAV8 and AAV10; clade F: AAV9).[63](#bib63) AAV4 was classified as a clone and later suggested to form clade G together with AAV11 and AAV12.[38](#bib38) Similarly, AAV5 was classified as a clone, which in the AAV community is sometimes assigned to clade H along with nonprimate AAVs such as AAVgo.1.[64](#bib64)

As mentioned above, AAV2 was the first AAV serotype whose capsid was structurally characterized.[46](#bib46) Since then, all thirteen AAV serotype capsid structures have been determined except for AAV10.[38](#bib38),[57](#bib57),[65](#bib65),[66](#bib66),[67](#bib67),[68](#bib68),[69](#bib69) However, the structural portfolio was complemented by AAVrh.39, which differs from AAV10 by only a single aa substitution (A589T) in the VP3 region.[70](#bib70) In addition, the capsid structures of AAVrh.8, AAVrh.10, AAVrh.4282, AAVhu.37, and AAVhu.69 have been determined[70](#bib70),[71](#bib71),[72](#bib72),[73](#bib73),[74](#bib74) ([Table S1](#mmc1)). While the aa sequence identity of primate AAV capsids ranges from 51% to 99%,[38](#bib38) their capsids may appear identical to the untrained eye. However, a distinguishable feature of these capsids is the shape of the 3-fold protrusions. These can protrude radially further outward and appear more “pointed,” as in the case of AAV2, or be radially shorter and more “rounded,” as seen in the AAV5 capsid ([Figure 3](#fig3)A), due to differences in loop conformations, deletions, and/or insertions in the surface loops. This results in AAV2 being one of the largest AAV capsids in terms of its maximum diameter (∼30 nm) and AAV5 one of the smaller AAV capsids (∼28 nm). However, the diameters at the 2-fold depression are essentially the same for both capsids (∼23 nm). These structural differences can be further visualized when the VP monomers are superposed using secondary structure matching algorithms[75](#bib75) ([Figure 3](#fig3)B). While the core of the capsids, with their secondary structure elements, are nearly identical for all primate-based AAVs, significant structural differences are observed in their surface loops. These similarities and differences result in an average root-mean-square deviation of the Cα atom positions (Cα RMSD) of ∼0.8 Å for the VP structures of the 18 primate AAV capsids.

## The variable regions of the AAVs

In 2006, the determination of the second capsid structure (AAV4) enabled structural comparison between two different AAVs.[66](#bib66) Using secondary structure matching, the VP3 models of AAV2 and AAV4 were superposed, resulting in an overall Cα RMSD of 1.0 Å.[66](#bib66) While the capsid core showed nearly exact overlap of both structures’ coordinates, significant positional differences were observed in the surface loops. Nine regions of structural variability were identified between the superposed capsids, defined as two or more consecutive aa with Cα position displacements greater than 1 Å apart. The nine variable regions (VRs) were originally numbered with Roman numerals; however, some publications also use Arabic numerals.[38](#bib38),[76](#bib76) The locations of the VRs within the VP structures have remained consistent even after the determination of many additional AAV capsid structures ([Figure 3](#fig3)B; [Table S2](#mmc1)) and are as follows: VR-I is located in the BC-loop, VR-II in the DE-loop, VR-III in the EF-loop, VR-IV to -VIII in the large GH-loop, and VR-IX near the C terminus following the βI-strand ([Figure 4](#fig4)). Within the capsid, VR-I, -III, and -XI form the 2/5-fold wall; VR-II forms the channel at the 5-fold symmetry axes; VR-IV, -V, and -VIII interact with each other to form the 3-fold protrusions; and VR-VI and -VII are located at the base of the 3-fold protrusions.

It should be noted that if the first description of the VRs had been based on a comparison of the AAV2 and AAV5 capsid structures, the HI-loop would have been included among the VRs, whereas VR-VIII would not, as this loop does not meet the definition given above for these AAVs.[57](#bib57) Thus, this review revisits the VRs across the full panel of primate AAVs for which capsid structures have been determined. For this purpose, the VP structures of 18 unique AAV capsids ([Figure 3](#fig3)B) were superposed to identify the first and last aa of each VR where at least one capsid shows a divergence of ≥ 1Å in its Cα aa position within the loop structure. As before, only stretches of more than two consecutive aa with this divergence were considered VRs.[66](#bib66) Due to the larger number of AAV structures now available, the VR aa ranges have expanded from the previous description ([Table S2](#mmc1)). The VRs are the segments of the VP3 sequences that exhibit the highest aa diversity within the capsid when compared across all AAVs and serve as determinants of their cell and tissue tropism as well as differential antigenic properties. However, the aa differences are not uniformly distributed. Some surface loops, such as VR-II, -III, and the HI-loop, are more conserved, as indicated by the larger letter sizes in the frequency plots, while others, such as VR-IV and VR-VIII, are highly variable ([Figure 5](#fig5)). Additionally, variations in loop length among the AAVs contribute to the structural heterogeneity of the VRs, whereas loops of the same length tend to have more similar loop conformations (e.g., VR-II and VR-VIII). The most pronounced structural variations are often observed at the apices of the VRs. However, some VRs, such as VR-IV, VR-V, and VR-IX, do not only have a single apex but are composed of two sub-loops. Among the analyzed capsids, AAV5 has the highest aa divergence from the other AAVs, which often results in unique loop conformations (e.g., VR-I, VR-V, VR-VII, and HI-loop, [Figure 5](#fig5): gray ribbon). Furthermore, clade-specific loop conformations are observed (e.g., for AAV4, AAV11, and AAV12 in VR-I, VR-IV, VR-V, and -VRVI, [Figure 3](#fig3): red, burgundy, and salmon ribbons). Finally, an analysis of the average aa composition for each loop showed that VR-VI has the highest number of charged aa, due to the presence of the prominent H-K-D-D-E/D-E/D-K/R sequence motif (aa526-532) in most AAVs. Particularly, the substitution of these acidic aa negatively affects the transduction efficiency of AAV vectors.[77](#bib77) However, the exact function of this region is unknown. Substitution of basic residues with neutral or acidic aa has been shown to increase capsid stability in some capsids.[78](#bib78),[79](#bib79) In contrast to VR-VI, the loop of VR-III has the fewest charged aa. Regarding the percentage of hydrophobic aa, the VRs are comparable, ranging between ∼30% and 40%. While hydrophobicity in the surface loops is limited due to solvent exposure, the roles of surface-exposed hydrophobic residues in capsid assembly, stability, aggregation, receptor interaction, and transduction efficiency are not fully characterized.

## The capsid structures of nonprimate based AAVs

In addition to the primates AAVs, several other viruses of the genus *Dependoparvovirus* have been isolated from a wide range of vertebrates, including cattle, goats, pigs, sea lions, foxes, bats, rodents, birds, and reptiles.[64](#bib64),[80](#bib80),[81](#bib81),[82](#bib82),[83](#bib83),[84](#bib84),[85](#bib85),[86](#bib86),[87](#bib87),[88](#bib88) The first two identified nonprimate AAVs were bovine AAV (BAAV) and quail AAV (QAAV, formerly known as avian AAV) in the 1970s, which were found as contaminants of bovine adenovirus type 1 and in preparations of the Olson strain of quail bronchitis, an avian adenovirus, respectively.[89](#bib89),[90](#bib90) The nonprimate AAVs can be as divergent as AAV5 is from the other AAV serotypes. One example is bat AAV isolate 10HB (BtAAV-10HB), with a VP1 sequence identity ranging from 53% to 60% compared to AAV1–AAV13. In 2020, the BtAAV-10HB capsid was the first nonprimate AAV structure determined, at a resolution of 3.0 Å.[91](#bib91) Since then, the capsids of serpentine AAV (SAAV), QAAV, goat AAV isolate 1 (AAVgo.1), goose parvovirus (GPV), and the porcine isolates 1 and 6 (AAVpo.1 and AAVpo.6) have been structurally characterized[92](#bib92),[93](#bib93),[94](#bib94),[95](#bib95),[96](#bib96) ([Table S3](#mmc1)). As for other members of the *Dependoparvovirus* genus, these viruses are nonpathogenic, with the exception of GPV, which is considered the causative agent of Derzy’s disease in waterfowl.[97](#bib97) The VP1 aa sequence identities of the different nonprimate AAVs range between 47% and 94% when compared to AAV2 and AAV5 ([Figure 6](#fig6)A). Overall, the capsid structures of the nonprimate AAVs display the conserved features shared among all AAVs and parvoviruses in general, including a channel at the 5-fold symmetry axis, depressions at the 2-fold symmetry axes, and protrusions around the 3-fold symmetry axes ([Figure 6](#fig6)B). The currently analyzed capsids have, for the most part, more rounded (AAV5-like) 3-fold protrusions, likely due to their shorter VR-IV loops ([Figure 6](#fig6)C). Similar to the primate AAVs, the VP structures show a high level of overlap, with the core of the capsids being nearly identical and structural variability primarily observed in the surface loops.

The nonprimate AAVs are being studied as alternative vectors for gene therapy applications, as pre-existing antibodies in the general human population exclude some patients from enrolling in AAV clinical trials. Currently, all approved AAV-based therapeutics are derived from primate AAVs. It was hypothesized that AAVs that do not disseminate in the human or primate population could circumvent pre-existing human antibodies. However, recent studies with human sera suggest a high level of cross-reactivity, with ∼25%–35% of a panel of human sera recognizing SAAV or QAAV.[92](#bib92),[93](#bib93) In most cases, the sera recognizing these AAVs also cross-reacted with most AAV serotypes, indicating that the highly conserved 5-fold region of the capsids is responsible. Similarly, a panel of human monoclonal antibodies obtained from Zolgensma recipients[98](#bib98) showed that antibodies targeting the 5-fold symmetry axes cross-react with several nonprimate-based AAV capsids.[93](#bib93),[95](#bib95),[96](#bib96) While some of these viruses are naturally able to transduce human cells or tissues[99](#bib99) others are unable to do so (e.g., QAAV). However, engineered QAAV capsids in which the VP1u region was swapped with that of AAV8 restored transduction in human cells.[100](#bib100) This strategy also worked with the capsids of SAAV and bearded dragon parvovirus (BDPV).[100](#bib100) Overall, the nonprimate AAVs are understudied, and only a small fraction of dependoparvoviruses has been characterized for their potential as future gene therapy vectors.

## Mapping the capsid’s interactions

The ability of AAV vectors to deliver their payload to target cells is determined by a series of interactions between the capsid and components of the immune system, cell attachment factors or surface receptors, as well as intracellular trafficking proteins that enable the transport of the transgene to the nucleus. These interactions are being characterized to obtain insights into the capsids’ functions and to improve the efficiency and specificity of AAV vectors. One of the most significant hurdles to the broad utilization of AAV vectors is the presence of pre-existing neutralizing antibodies (NAbs) in a large percentage of healthy individuals. These antibodies originate from prior infection with naturally circulating AAVs. Antibodies targeting the capsid can inactivate the vectors and lead to a loss of treatment efficacy. Thus, patients with NAbs and/or those exceeding defined antibody titer thresholds are excluded from receiving AAV therapeutics.[101](#bib101),[102](#bib102) A strategy to circumvent these pre-existing NAbs is the engineering of AAV capsids capable of evading this immune response. Prior to the “resolution revolution” in cryo-EM, the binding sites of mouse monoclonal antibodies were mapped to the capsids of AAV1, AAV2, AAV4, AAV5, AAV6, AAV8, AAV9, and AAVrh.10 at resolutions ranging from ∼5 to 20 Å.[103](#bib103),[104](#bib104),[105](#bib105),[106](#bib106),[107](#bib107),[108](#bib108),[109](#bib109),[110](#bib110),[111](#bib111),[112](#bib112) At these resolutions, models of previously determined high-resolution capsid and antibody structures were fitted into the lower-resolution maps to identify a shortlist of potential aa in the capsid epitope for the analyzed antibody. The improvement of the cryo-EM technology enabled the direct identification of the contact aa on the capsid surface that interact with the complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) of the fragment antigen-binding (Fab) domains of antibodies at high resolution. The first high-resolution AAV-antibody complex structure was that of AAV5 with the mouse monoclonal antibody HL2476, which binds to the capsid’s 3-fold protrusions[113](#bib113) ([Table S4](#mmc1)). More recently, the complex structures of a panel of 21 human monoclonal antibodies, derived from three patients who received the biologic Zolgensma, bound to the AAV9 capsid were determined.[114](#bib114) Among these 21 complex structures, the vast majority (>75%) of the antibodies bound near the 2-fold region of the capsid, with two antibodies binding to the 3- and 5-fold regions each, and another one to the 2/5-fold wall (Fab1-2, [Figure 7](#fig7)A). Another observation from these structures was that ligands binding at or close to the symmetry axes of the capsid cannot be resolved by applying global icosahedral symmetry during 3D image reconstruction. Instead, localized reconstruction of sub-particles for the region of interest is required to resolve the ligands without “blurring.” The interface area for these antibodies ranged between ∼1000 and 2000 Å2 (average: ∼1500 Å2) ([Figure 7](#fig7)A).

Similar to the Fabs of human or murine antibodies, the binding of single-chain camelid VH domain antibodies, also referred to as nanobodies,[115](#bib115) has been mapped to AAV capsids. These nanobodies are only about a quarter of the size of the Fab fragment of a standard IgG and are used in affinity chromatography purification protocols, enabling scalable "Good Manufacturing Practice" purification of AAV vectors. The most commonly utilized nanobodies, AVB and AAVX, enable the purification of a wide range of AAV capsids.[116](#bib116),[117](#bib117) Their binding sites have been mapped at high resolution to the AAV8 capsid (AVB: 2.7 Å, AAVX: 2.3 Å) ([Figure 7](#fig7)B; [Table S4](#mmc1)) and at lower resolution (4–9 Å) to the capsids of AAV1 (AVB and AAVX), AAV2, and AAV5 (only AVB).[118](#bib118),[119](#bib119) Both bind to the 5-fold region of the capsids and are structurally nearly identical but differ in their ability to purify the capsids of AAV9.[116](#bib116),[117](#bib117) Additionally, nanobodies specifically for the purification of AAV8 and AAV9 have been developed. Cryo-EM structures of these ligands bound to their respective capsids at ∼3–4 Å resolution show them interacting with the 2/5-fold wall (Capture Select AAV8) or the 5-fold region (Capture Select AAV9).[118](#bib118) Due to their smaller size, the interface area of the nanobodies with the AAV capsids is usually smaller than that of human or murine IgGs ([Figure 7](#fig7)B). These complex structures identified the critical capsid aa required for purification of an AAV sample and will guide future capsid engineering efforts to ensure compatibility of new AAV vectors with affinity purification resins.

As with antibodies, several molecules such as glycan and proteinaceous receptors have been complexed with AAV capsids to further understand the vectors’ cell and tissue tropism. The binding sites of several protein receptors have been determined structurally. One membrane protein that is important for the transduction of many AAVs is KIAA0319L, also known as AAVR.[120](#bib120) Its extracellular portion contains five Ig-like polycystic kidney disease (PKD) domains. Constructs comprising PKD1-5 or PKD1-2 have been complexed with the capsids of AAV1, -2, -5, -9, AAVgo.1, and the engineered capsid PHP.eB (see [the capsid structures of engineered AAVs](#sec7) section), and cryo-EM structures have been determined at resolutions ranging from 2.4 to 3.8 Å.[94](#bib94),[121](#bib121),[122](#bib122),[123](#bib123),[124](#bib124),[125](#bib125),[126](#bib126) For AAV1, -2, -9, and PHP.eB, the PKD2 domain of AAVR interacted with the capsids in the same binding mode, along the side of the 3-fold protrusions and on top of the 2/5-fold wall ([Figure 7](#fig7)C), whereas AAV5 and AAVgo.1 both bound to the PKD1 domain around the 5-fold axis of the capsids toward the 2/5-fold wall. Another membrane protein complexed with an AAV capsid is carbonic anhydrase 4 (Car4). This protein is anchored to the cell surface via a glycosylphosphatidylinositol linkage,[127](#bib127) which was identified as a potential receptor for the engineered capsids AAV9-P31 (see [the capsid structures of engineered AAVs](#sec7) section) and AAV9-P36.[128](#bib128) Recombinant Car4 was found to bind to the 3-fold protrusions of AAV9-P31. Due to its size, similar to antibodies bound close to the symmetry axis, a localized cryo-EM reconstruction approach was needed to resolve the complex at 1.8 Å resolution.[129](#bib129) Recently, the transmembrane protein carboxypeptidase D, also referred to as AAVR2, was identified as an alternative receptor for AAV8.[130](#bib130) The binding site of AAVR2 was mapped to the AAV8 capsid in the same study, which showed it interacting with the 3-fold protrusions across the 2-fold symmetry axes at a resolution of 2.9 Å.

Currently, all high-resolution cryo-EM structures for capsid complexes are determined using single-particle reconstructions, which involve the structural averaging of a large number of homogeneous particles. However, the flexible nature of some proteins interacting with the AAV capsid using this technique results in them being averaged out and thus not detectable. Some studies have turned to cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) to reveal these dynamic interactions, but technical limitations restrict the achievable resolution.[131](#bib131) The first application of cryo-ET analyzed the binding of the PKD1-PKD2 domain of AAVR to the AAV2 and AAV5 capsids.[126](#bib126) The resulting ∼20 Å structures revealed four potential configurations of the PKD1 domain in the case of the AAV2 capsid and the tightly bound PKD2 domain. However, the flexible PKD1 configurations are all different from those seen in AAV5. For the AAV5-PKD1-PKD2 complex, PKD1 binds tightly, but the sub-tomograms showed three conformations of the previously missing PKD2 domain extending away from the surface of the capsid. In another study, cryo-ET was used to determine the binding site of human interleukin 3 (IL3) at the side of the 3-fold protrusion adjacent to the 2-fold depression on the AAV9 capsid.[132](#bib132) IL3 is an immunomodulatory protein produced by activated T cells, and thus this interaction has implications for the host immune response and tolerance when receiving AAV-based gene therapy treatments.

Lastly, the binding modes of AAV6 and AAVpo.1 to importin alpha (IMPα) were determined using X-ray crystallography.[133](#bib133),[134](#bib134) This interaction is mediated by the structurally disordered region within the VP1u and VP1/2 common region; thus, only a short segment (aa115–174) was utilized for the complex instead of the full capsid. In this structure, IMPα interacted with the nuclear localization signals (BR1 and BR3) of the tested AAVs. At the end of the intracellular trafficking pathway, IMPα is responsible for the import of AAV capsids into the nucleus, and understanding this interaction may provide opportunities for developing engineered AAV vectors with improved nuclear import characteristics.

Many of the AAVs have been shown to utilize glycans for cell surface attachment.[107](#bib107),[135](#bib135),[136](#bib136),[137](#bib137),[138](#bib138),[139](#bib139),[140](#bib140),[141](#bib141) While some of their binding sites were characterized by mutational analysis, others were identified structurally. For sialic acid (SIA), the binding sites on the AAV1 and AAV5 capsids were determined by X-ray crystallography[142](#bib142),[143](#bib143) and for SAAV by cryo-EM.[92](#bib92) In each of these complex maps, SIA bound differently to the capsids: at the base of the 3-fold protrusions in the case of AAV1 ([Figure 7](#fig7)D), in proximity to the 3-fold axis for AAV5, and on the 2/5-fold wall in the SAAV capsid. Heparin or related analogs have been mapped to the capsids of AAV2 and AAV3 at low resolution, showing their binding at or near the capsids’ 3-fold-protrusion.[144](#bib144),[145](#bib145),[146](#bib146) Similarly, a synthetic heparinoid was complexed with the engineered AAV-DJ capsid (see [the capsid structures of engineered AAVs](#sec7) section) by cryo-EM at 2.8 Å resolution, showing density for the glycan at the apices of the 3-fold protrusions.[147](#bib147) For the AAV9 capsid complexed with a terminal galactose glycan and the AAVrh.10 capsid with a sulfated LacNAc tetrasaccharide, cryo-EM structures at resolutions ranging from 2.4–3.1 Å showed density at the base of the 3-fold protrusions,[107](#bib107),[148](#bib148) the same pocket where AAV1 and AAV6 bind to SIA molecules ([Figure 7](#fig7)D).[142](#bib142) Overall, the AAV capsids predominantly interact with glycans and proteinaceous receptors at or near their 3-fold protrusions and the 2/5-fold wall, which generally display greater aa and structural diversity among the AAVs, resulting in varying host, tissue, and cell tropism. # ColabFold

Paste a sequence and get a predicted structure back, with per-residue confidence. Trades a little accuracy for speed by skipping the search for related natural sequences.

## What it is for

You have a sequence and want its 3D shape quickly, trading a little accuracy for speed. It skips the search for related natural sequences that full AlphaFold2 runs. Use it to triage a batch; use AlphaFold2 when the answer has to be right.

Predicts a structure from a sequence by skipping the search for related natural sequences that full AlphaFold2 runs. Same AlphaFold2 weights, less evidence to work from — so a little less accurate and a lot faster. Useful for triaging a batch of sequences or getting a quick look at a well-behaved fold. ColabFold, Mirdita et al., *Nature Methods* 2022.

When it fits:

-   You want a structure quickly and can live with slightly less accuracy than full AlphaFold2.
-   You are folding a batch of sequences one after another and throughput matters more than the last few points of confidence.
-   Your target is a well-behaved single chain or small complex with no unusual chemistry.

## Inputs

You will need:

-   Single-letter FASTA sequence(s).
-   Targets with deep evolutionary signal. Multi-domain or low-information sequences underperform without MSA.

Each run uses a preset that sets the scale and scope:

Standalone with your FASTA

Paste a FASTA (monomer or multimer up to 600 aa total) and get pLDDT, PAE, and pTM/ipTM. Runs on an A100-40GB. No MSA, no templates. Pair with D2 AF2 if you need the full MSA-backed fold.

Batch for many fold targets

Fold many independent targets in one job (up to 200 records). Each record can be a monomer or a multimer (use \`\`:\`\` inside a record to break chains). Per-design results stream into the job page as folds complete. Fast no-MSA tier.

Parameters you set on the form:

Sequence

Paste FASTA. Use `:` as a chain separator for multimers.

Recycles

Model recycles. ColabFold default is 3; reduce for speed if your target's fold is well-known.

## How to read the results

Predicted PDB with per-residue pLDDT and PAE, plus pTM and ipTM on a multimer. An ipTM of 0.6 or more is a plausible interface and 0.75 or more is strong. On a run of your own the structure downloads from the results page. The PAE matrix downloads only from a standalone run — a batch returns no PAE file.

Where a tool reports them, the scores mean:

ipTM

Predicted confidence in the contact between two chains, on a 0 to 1 scale. Higher is better: 0.65 to 0.75 depending on the tool. Individual tools set their own pass bar a little either side of that — this guide's own results summary above states this tool's. On a multi-chain target the number may cover the target's own chain–chain interface as well as the binder's, so read the per-tool note on the results table before comparing designs on it.

pLDDT

Per-residue confidence in the predicted fold. Higher means the model is more sure of that part of the structure.

i\_pAE and pAE

Predicted alignment error, at the interface (i\_pAE) or across the whole structure (pAE). Lower is better.

## References

Mirdita et al., Nature Methods 2022

# GROMACS 2024.1 on brand-new GPGPUs

![A close-up picture of super computer racks.](https://hpc.fau.de/files/2024/08/News-Story-Cromacs-1024x576.png)

The first patch for the newest GROMACS version 2024 was released end of February. Recently, several new GPGPUs were added to the test cluster at NHR@FAU. As we benchmarked our usual set of six simulation systems, we decided to write a follow-up on our GROMACS benchmark posts ([Multi-GPU GROMACS Jobs on TinyGPU](https://hpc.fau.de/2021/06/18/multi-gpu-gromacs-jobs-on-tinygpu/) and [GROMACS performance on different GPU types](https://hpc.fau.de/2022/02/10/gromacs-performance-on-different-gpu-types/)) due to some interesting results on the latest hardware.

## **The Benchmarks**

1.  [R-143a in hexane](https://hpc.fau.de/files/2022/02/r-143a-in-hexane-nhr-fau.zip) (20,248 atoms) with very high output rate,
2.  a short [RNA piece with explicit water](https://hpc.fau.de/files/2022/02/rnanvt-nhr-fau.zip) (31,889 atoms),
3.  a [protein inside a membrane](https://hpc.fau.de/files/2022/02/membrane-protein-rrze-nhr-fau.zip) surrounded by explicit water (80,289 atoms),
4.  a [protein in explicit water](https://hpc.fau.de/files/2022/02/protein-explicit-water-nhr-fau.zip) (170,320 atoms),
5.  a [protein membrane channel](https://github.com/PDC-support/benchmarks-procurement/tree/master/benchmarks/GROMACS) with explicit water (615,924 atoms), and
6.  a huge [virus protein](https://zenodo.org/record/3893789) (1,066,628 atoms).

For running these benchmarks with GROMACS 2024.1 on a GPU, the following command was executed:

$ gmx mdrun -v -s $benchmark.tpr -nb gpu -pme gpu -bonded gpu -update gpu -ntmpi 1 -ntomp 16 -pin on \\
   -pinstride 1 -nsteps 200000 -deffnm $benchmark\_name

This offloads all possible calculations to the GPU and pins the program threads to CPU cores; the number of OpenMP threads depends on how many CPU cores are available. Since several GPUs are combined with one host CPU in Alex, each GPU has access to only a fraction of the host, which on Alex is 16 cores. The flags `‑nsteps`, `‑v`, and `‑deffnm` are used for convenient benchmarking purposes and are not recommended in production runs; especially `‑v` should only be used for debugging.
